description_full: Apple Inc. designs, manufactures, and markets smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables, and accessories. The company offers iPhone, a line of smartphones; Mac, a line of personal computers; iPad, a line of multi-purpose tablets; and wearables, home, and accessories, including Apple Watch, AirPods, Beats products, Apple Vision Pro, Apple TV 4K, HomePod, and Apple HomeView, as well as Apple branded and third-party accessories. It also provides advertising services comprising third-party licensing arrangements and own advertising platforms; AppleCare and cloud services; and payment services, including Apple Card and Apple Pay. In addition, the company operates App Store that allow customers to discover and download applications and digital content, such as books, music, video, games, and podcasts. Further, it provides digital content through subscription-based services, including Apple Arcade, a game service; Apple Fitness+, a personalized fitness service; Apple Music, which offers users a curated listening experience; Apple News+, a news and magazine service; and Apple TV, which offers original content and live sports. The company sells its products and resells third-party products through its retail and online stores, and direct sales force; its services through its various service platforms; and third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers. It serves consumer, small and mid-sized business, education, enterprise, and government markets. The company operates in North and South America, European countries, India, the Middle East, Africa, China mainland, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Japan, Australia, New Zealand, and rest of Asia. The company was formerly known as Apple Computer, Inc. and changed its name to Apple Inc. in January 2007. Apple Inc. was founded in 1976 and is headquartered in Cupertino, California.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 167K people. Revenue per employee of $2.9M ranks in the top quartile among Technology peers, improving at 16%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $815K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $83K per employee reflects an ownership culture. Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (6/10).
financial_summary: Apple Inc. is a mega-cap technology business with a $5.0T market cap on $478.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 89% against a 10% cost of capital — a 79-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 40%.

The business throws off $136.1B in free cash flow — roughly 28 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.10× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.1× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 29× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sect: Its 33% operating margin runs 26pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.41x).
It accounts for 10.8% of sector revenue and 15.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-10.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 24% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 4% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 25% and a beta of 1.12, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.65 vs 5y 1.14), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $12.6B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 31% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 60% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $246 (margin of safety -39%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 25%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $173 to $354 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 38.1 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 29.4 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 36.6 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 61% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 39 covering analysts target $333 on average, 3% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 89% clears the cost of capital of 10.2% by 79pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.52).
It runs a 40% gross margin and converts 28% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 9/9 and cash conversion of 1.10x.
ROE of 118% is amplified by 3.6x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 9.6% of revenue on R&D and 2.9% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.1x net debt to EBITDA ($56.7B of cash against $80.1B of debt), with interest covered 29.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 12.7, in the safe zone).
It runs on negative working capital (-67 days), so customers and suppliers effectively fund its operations.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.7% over 3 years, 5.5% over 5 years and 8.3% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 24%).
At current returns, reinvesting 13% of profits supports about 11.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 7.9% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (1.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 31, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.7%, and institutions hold 67%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (27 sales, net $94.4M sold).
It returns 2.1% a year to shareholders (1.7% in buybacks and 0.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 14 consecutive years, raising it 1.7% a year over the last five.
people: With about 167,000 employees, each generates about $2.9M of revenue, 7.7x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 16.3% a year.
That works out to $815K of free cash flow per employee.
